title: How does garbage collection work and what are generations in .NET?
description: Understand the .NET garbage collector and generational optimization.

data.text: **Question:** How does garbage collection work and what are generations in .NET?

The .NET Garbage Collector (GC) automatically manages memory by reclaiming unused objects. It uses generational collection: Gen 0 for new objects, Gen 1 for short-lived survivors, and Gen 2 for long-lived objects. This optimizes collection frequency and performance.

**How GC Works:**
- Tracing garbage collector (not reference counting)
- Identifies objects no longer reachable from roots
- Compacts memory to reduce fragmentation
- Runs automatically when memory pressure occurs
- Can be triggered manually with GC.Collect() (rarely needed)

**Generations:**
- **Gen 0:** Newly created objects, collected frequently
- **Gen 1:** Objects surviving Gen 0 collection, buffer between short and long-lived
- **Gen 2:** Long-lived objects, collected infrequently
- Larger heap = longer collection time

**GC Modes:**
- **Workstation:** For desktop apps, concurrent GC
- **Server:** For server apps, one GC per CPU core
- **Background:** Concurrent with application threads

data.takeaway: The generational GC optimizes performance by focusing on young objects, which are most likely to be garbage.
